extracted.intended_audience: readers of literary criticism and American literary history; aspiring writers and students of 19th-century American letters
extracted.subtask_description: First-person essays recollecting encounters with late-19th/early-20th-century American authors and reflecting on what counted as literary quality and reputation in that era. Mixes memoir, critical judgment, and cultural context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication imprint as warrant of quality
rubrics_metrics.description: "Their imprint was a warrant of quality to the reader and of immortality to the author" (referring to Ticknor & Fields).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Howells argues that being published by recognized houses or periodicals (e.g., Atlantic Monthly; Ticknor & Fields) functioned as an external guarantee of literary quality and permanence — young writers coveted those outlets and judged peers by such publication credentials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different dimensions of greatness among authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Longfellow was "easily the greatest poet of the three, Holmes often the most brilliant and felicitous, but Lowell... the finest scholar and the most profoundly literary, as he was... most deeply and thoroughly New England in quality."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literary excellence is multi-dimensional (greatness of poetic gift, brilliance/wit, scholarly depth, regional authenticity). Evaluation should note which kind of strength an author exhibits rather than treating 'greatness' as a single property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional character shapes literary value
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated emphasis that New England furnished a distinct intellectual life and that some authors (e.g., Lowell) are 'thoroughly New England in quality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The cultural and regional roots of an author (New England vs. New York vs. the West) are treated as meaningful criteria for understanding style, themes, and literary importance; critics should attend to locality and its influence on a work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodical publication and editorial platforms as career criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Young writers were ambitious to join names 'in the Atlantic Monthly' and periodicals were central to literary life; the Atlantic's office was imagined as the locus of accessibility to authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Access to particular journals and magazines is presented as a practical and reputational criterion for an author's standing; editors and periodicals shape what is seen as acceptable or prestigious literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public persona, lecturing, and performance contribute to reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: "That was the heyday of lecturing... a literary light from the East swam into our skies. I heard and saw Emerson..." — public lecturing and personal presence mattered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An author's public activity (lectures, appearances) and personal comportment form part of how contemporaries evaluate literary worth and influence; critical accounts should include how performance shaped reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly labor and translation as marks of distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Bayard Taylor's 'incomparable translation of Faust' and his late study of Greek are cited as examples of scholarly accomplishment that enhance an author's standing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deep scholarship and serious translation work are presented as significant contributions to a writer's reputation — critics may weigh erudition and cross-cultural engagement when assessing value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional sincerity and tonal qualities in poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Howells notes the 'pathetic romance of his early love' as a quality that made certain poetry especially appealing even when it 'paid the inevitable allegiance to the manner of the great masters.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic merit includes genuine feeling, melodic or romantic appeal, and successful emotional expression; originality may be tempered by mannerism, but sincerity and beauty remain valuable criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of subject and local sensitivity affect reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Hawthorne's treatment of his native Salem caused coolness among locals; 'the advantages to any place of having a great genius born and reared in its midst are so doubtful' — local sentiment can judge an author's work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers who use recognizable local subjects risk alienating that community; critics should consider how an author's material choices interact with local pride, memory, and propriety when assessing effects and reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary taste is shaped by foreign and prior authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Young writers 'accepted the Saturday Review as law' and looked to England and Europe for opinions; tastes were formed by reading Thackeray, George Eliot, Hawthorne, Tennyson, Heine, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitative influence and reliance on established critical authorities are an important factor in how writers and critics form judgments; assessors should note lineage of influence when evaluating originality and quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal ambition, modesty, and self-presentation influence literary beginnings
rubrics_metrics.description: Howells describes his own youthful mix of modesty and ambition (veins 'might well have run ink rather than blood') and episodes of awkwardness in encountering famous authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An author's early public demeanor, self-promotion or modesty, and social positioning can affect opportunities and early reception; while not a direct aesthetic criterion, these personal factors influence career trajectories and the formation of reputations.
